h1:
First Time in Chumphon
What to Know
intro: Chumphon is the gateway to the south that a lot of people just drive through or use as a stop on the way to Koh Tao. But the place actually has it all — white-sand beaches, a shrine the whole province reveres, island diving, homegrown robusta coffee, and fresh seafood straight from local fishermen — at prices that are still easy on the wallet. If this is your first time, this guide pulls together everything worth knowing before you go: how to get there, when to visit, what you shouldn't miss, what to eat, what to take home, and it wraps up with a 2-day 1-night plan you can actually follow.

blocks.html: Honestly, Chumphon isn't a town built to flatter tourists with a selfie sign on every corner. Its charm is that it's a coastal town that still lives a real life — fishing boats come and go from the pier every morning, the markets serve bold southern flavors, and the sea hasn't been overrun the way Samui or Krabi have. The upside is quiet and cheap; the trade-off is that the sights are spread far apart and public transport is thin. Knowing your way around ahead of time makes the trip a lot more fun, so we've put everything first-timers usually get confused about on one page.

Chumphon sits about 460 km from Bangkok, and there are several ways down — each suited to a different kind of traveler. The thing first-timers should know is that once you reach Chumphon, you still have to get around inside the province, because the sights are scattered along the coast rather than clustered in town.

items: Train — the Southern Line from Hua Lamphong/Bang Sue gets off at Chumphon Station, taking about 7–9 hours. Take the overnight sleeper and you wake up right as you arrive, saving a night's accommodation.
Coach — from the new Southern Bus Terminal, around 7–8 hours, dropping you in town, with plenty of departures day and night.
Plane — flights land at Chumphon Airport, about 1 hour 10 minutes from Don Muang. Fastest option, but flights don't run every hour, so check the schedule first.
Driving yourself — head south down Phetkasem Road. The smoothest choice, since you've got a car ready to explore the province right away.

blocks.title: If you're connecting on to Koh Tao
blocks.html: Lots of people use Chumphon as a stopover up to Koh Tao. The main pier is near Ao Thung Makham Noi, about 28 km from town, and the catamaran takes roughly 1 hour 45 minutes, with the morning run usually leaving around 07:00. There's a shuttle from the train station to the pier that you can book bundled with your ticket. If you want to see a bit of Chumphon too, leave a night before catching the boat — don't book the boat for the same day your train arrives on a tight schedule.

blocks.title: Book the activities in your Chumphon trip ahead
blocks.text: Booking online ahead on Klook or GetYourGuide is usually cheaper than the gate and skips the queue. Pick only the experiences you actually want — prices and availability are shown live on each site.

items.label: Day trips from Chumphon
items.note: Out and back in a day

blocks.html: This matters more than you'd think, because Chumphon sits on the Gulf of Thailand side, where the monsoon brings waves strong enough that some days the dive boats can't go out. If you've come specifically to dive the islands, timing is everything.

items: February–May — clear water, low swells, the best window for island diving, with open skies and a beautiful sea.
June–September — rain alternating with sun; still doable, fewer people, cheaper rooms, but you're gambling on intermittent showers.

October–January — Gulf monsoon season, strong waves, and some days the boats can't run, so focus on land, cafes, and temples instead · October brings the migrating hawk-watching festival at Khao Din So, the highlight of this stretch.

blocks.text: Sights You Shouldn't Miss the First Time

blocks.html: If it's your first time and you're short on time, you don't need to hit everything — pick from this list based on what you're into. Most of it is over by Mueang district and Sai Ri Beach, which are close together and can be done in a single day's drive. Pathio is farther north, so save it for the second day or your next trip.

items.name: Sai Ri Beach + Krom Luang Chumphon Shrine
items.blurb: A white-sand beach with clear water, about 20 km from town. On the rise by the shore stands the shrine of Krom Luang Chumphon Khet Udomsak — "Sadej Tia" — revered across the whole province, with a model warship and a wide sea view. This is the first pin locals tell you to hit.

items.name: Chumphon Islands Diving
items.blurb: Take a boat out to snorkel at Koh Ran Ped and Koh Ngam Noi/Ngam Yai — clear water, plenty of fish, and a shot at spotting a whale shark. It's the province's highlight that outsiders still haven't covered, so book the tour ahead and check the wind.

items.name: Pak Nam Chumphon
items.blurb: A river-mouth fishing community where you can watch boats coming and going from the pier and eat fresh seafood by the water at good prices. The evening atmosphere is lovely, and it's a popular dinner spot for visitors.

items.name: Thung Wua Laen Beach (Pathio)
items.blurb: A long, pretty stretch of sand up in Pathio district — shallow water, gentle waves, good for swimming and bringing kids. It's far north of town, so it suits people with a full day or a 3-day extension.

items.name: Khao Din So + Viewpoint
items.blurb: A sea viewpoint over in Pathio. In October, hundreds of thousands of migrating hawks pass overhead — a natural phenomenon photographers come specifically to catch. The rest of the year you can still come up for the coastal view.

items.name: Wat Khao Chedi + Pathio Tree Tunnel
items.blurb: A hilltop temple with sea views all around, plus a tree-lined road that curves into a green tunnel people love stopping to photograph. Both are in the Pathio zone, so you can pair them with Thung Wua Laen in one day.

blocks.html: The food is the reason a lot of people come back. Chumphon shines at fresh seafood from local fishermen, bold southern dishes, and robusta coffee grown in the province itself. The list below is the spots people talk about that fit a route around town and Sai Ri, ordered by when you'd likely stop in rather than which one is better than another. Check the closing days and hours again before you go, just to be safe.

items.name: Southern Khanom Jeen Nam Ya — Chumphon Morning Market
items.blurb: A proper southern breakfast: rice noodles in bold crab nam ya, eaten with fresh raw veggies on the side. It's a light, local way to open the day before heading out, and the morning market has plenty of other southern dishes to choose from.
items.meta: Morning market in town · open early to late morning

items.name: Krua Je Ang — Pak Nam Chumphon
items.blurb: A roadside seafood restaurant on the way to the Krom Luang shrine, with ingredients fresh from local fishermen. Lots of standout dishes — fried fish, sour curry, and spicy salads — making it a fitting lunch stop on the Sai Ri Beach route.
items.meta: Pak Nam Chumphon · on the way to Sai Ri Beach

items.name: Mae Mai Seafood
items.blurb: A seafood restaurant along the Chumphon–Pak Nam road with an easy atmosphere and a full seafood menu — blue crab, prawns, squid. It's a place locals often bring guests.

items.name: Krua Thung Phae
items.blurb: A leafy garden seafood spot with several seating areas to choose from, great for coming with a group and settling in for a relaxed long meal. Plenty of seafood and made-to-order dishes to pick from.

items.name: Chaloem Chill Lay
items.blurb: A chilled-out seaside seafood place where you sit with fresh seafood and a cold drink catching the breeze. Good for dinner if you want a sea view to close out the day.

items.name: Robusta Station
items.blurb: A minimalist cafe along Phetkasem Road using well-selected Chumphon robusta beans, with local goods to take home like roasted coffee beans, southern curries, and dried products. Handy for grabbing a coffee and stocking up on souvenirs in one place.
items.price: Coffee from low hundreds THB · souvenirs priced separately

items.name: Rolly Café
items.blurb: A small seaside cafe with its own little roastery, so you get freshly roasted coffee and a rotating selection of foreign beans. Easygoing atmosphere, good for a break after coming back from the sea.
items.meta: Seaside · check the hours before you go

items.name: Chumphon Night Market
items.blurb: Wallet-friendly dinner with savory and sweet bites and fried snacks — plenty to graze on for a while. Good for the first night if you want a relaxed, cheap meal near your accommodation.
items.meta: In Chumphon town · open evening to late

blocks.html: Before you leave, leave time for a souvenir stop. The popular spot is the Por Ta Hin Chang shrine on Phetkasem Road just before you exit the province, where souvenir shops line up so you can get everything in one stop. There aren't many signature items, but the good ones are genuinely good.

items: Dried lady-finger bananas — Chumphon's small bananas, baked or sun-dried until sweet and chewy, the province's number-one souvenir.
Chumphon robusta coffee — 100% roasted beans grown in the province, available in several roast levels from light to dark, sold as beans or ground.
Processed seafood — dried squid, dried shrimp, chili dips — dried goods from the sea that travel home easily.
Durian and seasonal fruit — Chumphon is a fruit town; during durian season (roughly May–August) you can taste and buy it fresh by the roadside.

blocks.html: If it's your first time and you've got about two days, this plan covers the highlights around town, Sai Ri, and the islands without running you ragged all day. Day one is an easy take on town and the beach; day two is an early dive boat that wraps up with coffee and souvenirs. Adjust the timing to suit yourself — we've slotted in real restaurants and real spots already.

blocks.label: Day 1
blocks.title: Town, Sai Ri Beach, the Krom Luang shrine, and Pak Nam seafood

items.activity: Head into Chumphon town for a breakfast of southern khanom jeen nam ya at the morning market, with a hot robusta coffee.
items.note: The morning market has plenty of southern dishes to choose from.

items.activity: Drive to Sai Ri Beach, stroll the shore, swim, or paddle a kayak.
Have lunch at a roadside seafood spot on the Sai Ri route, like Krua Je Ang or Mae Mai Seafood.
items.note: Fresh sea fish from local fishermen.

items.activity: Go up to pay respects at the Krom Luang Chumphon Khet Udomsak shrine, and see the model warship and wide sea view.
items.note: Dress modestly within the shrine grounds.

items.activity: Stop by the Chumphon Islands Nature Study Center and walk the mangrove boardwalk in the cool breeze.
items.note: Skippable if you'd rather check into your room first.

items.activity: Go to Pak Nam Chumphon for a waterfront seafood dinner and watch the fishing boats return to the pier.
items.note: The blue crab, grilled prawns, and grilled squid here are fresh and well-priced.

items.activity: Head back to your room and turn in early for an early start the next morning.

blocks.label: Day 2
blocks.title: Dive the Chumphon islands, then close the trip with coffee and souvenirs

items.activity: Check out and board the boat from the Sai Ri or Pak Nam pier, heading out to the islands.
items.note: Check the weather with the tour one more time before setting off.

items.activity: Snorkel at Koh Ran Ped and take in the large field of sea anemones.
items.note: This spot is the trip's highlight.

items.activity: Continue to Koh Ngam Noi and Ngam Yai — clear water, plenty of fish, and a shot at spotting a whale shark.
Have lunch on the boat or stop for crab on an island, depending on the tour package.
Head back to shore, rinse off, and change.
items.note: Leave a little buffer in case the boat returns slightly behind schedule.

items.activity: Stop by a robusta coffee cafe like Robusta Station for a coffee and buy roasted beans as a souvenir.
items.note: An easy way to close out the trip.

items.activity: Stop at the Por Ta Hin Chang shrine to pick up dried lady-finger bananas and souvenirs, then set off home.

blocks.title: If the weather doesn't cooperate on dive day
blocks.html: During monsoon season the boat might not be able to go out. If that happens, swap day two for a land trip instead: drive up to Pathio for Thung Wua Laen Beach, Khao Din So, or Wat Khao Chedi with its all-around sea views, stop at the tree tunnel for photos, then come back down to a cafe in town. It's a different vibe but still a full day.

blocks.text: Getting Around the Province and How to Prepare

blocks.html: The thing first-timers often get wrong is assuming that once you reach town, getting around is easy. In reality, Sai Ri Beach, Pak Nam, the pier, and Pathio are all in different directions, and public transport is scarce. There are songthaews and motorcycle taxis in town, but to head out of town you need your own ride.

items: Rent a vehicle in town — the smoothest option if you arrive by train or plane, since the sights are spread out.
Dive-day gear — swimsuit, towel, sunscreen, a waterproof phone pouch, and seasickness pills.
Footwear — strap sandals or water shoes, which handle rocks and boarding the boat better than flip-flops.
Cash — local shops and some boat tours mostly take cash, so it's better to have some on hand.
Book ahead — boat tours don't run on a fixed schedule and need booking in advance, and beachfront rooms fill up fast over long weekends.

faq.q: How many days do I need for a first visit to Chumphon?
faq.a: At least 2 days and 1 night is enough to cover the highlights around town, Sai Ri Beach, the Krom Luang shrine, and a day of island diving. If you also want to take in the Pathio side — Thung Wua Laen, Khao Din So, and the tree tunnel — you should allow 3 days and 2 nights, since the sights are far apart.

faq.q: Can I get around Chumphon without my own car?
faq.a: You can, but it's much easier if you rent a car or motorbike in town, because Sai Ri Beach, Pak Nam, the pier, and Pathio are far apart and public transport is thin. For the island trip, it's simpler to book a boat tour that includes a shuttle from your accommodation or town.

faq.q: When is the best time to visit Chumphon?
faq.a: February to May is the clear-water, low-swell window, the best for island diving. October to January is the Gulf monsoon season, with strong waves and some days the boats can't go out, so if you come then, focus on land trips and have a backup plan.

faq.q: What Chumphon souvenirs should I buy?
faq.a: The signature items are dried lady-finger bananas, the province's roasted robusta coffee, and processed seafood like dried squid and chili dips. You can stop at the Por Ta Hin Chang shrine on Phetkasem Road before leaving the province, where the shops line up so you can get everything in one place.

faq.q: Can I combine Chumphon with Koh Tao?
faq.a: Yes, Chumphon is a popular boat connection to Koh Tao. The pier is near Ao Thung Makham Noi, about 28 km from town, and the boat takes roughly 1 hour 45 minutes. It's worth spending a night in Chumphon before catching the boat — and don't book a boat departure tight against your train arrival time.
